newsitem.title: INDIA: Japanese business chiefs praise India reforms.
newsitem.headline: Japanese business chiefs praise India reforms.

text.p: A high-powered Japanese business mission on Friday applauded India's economic reforms and, in a change of tack, withdrew a demand that New Delhi amend labour laws to make them more friendly to foreign investors.

Toyota Motor Corp chairman Shoichiro Toyoda, head of Japan's influential Keidanren economic federation, said India had taken steps to assuage foreign investors' worries since the last Keidanren delegation gave New Delhi mixed marks in 1995.
"There has been some progress made since two years ago," Toyoda told a news conference in the Indian capital.

When Keidanren, an association of leading businesses and industries, last sent a delegation to India, it complained of poor technology, ailing technology and labour laws that discourages unprofitable firms from closing their doors.
"I think many problems have been resolved," Keidanren director general Masaya Miyoshi said.
In a shift of position, the Japanese delegation said it was no longer pressing India to overhaul labour laws so foreign investors could close inefficient plants.

"Given the employment situation in India, I don't think this is an issue that can be easily resolved," Miyoshi said, referring to high joblessness. "I do not believe that this issue remains a big problem for potential Japanese investors here."
Tarun Das, director general of the Confederation of Indian Industry, told Reuters the softening of the Japanese federation's stance on labour laws was significant.
While Japan is India's biggest official aid donor, it has lagged far behind the United States and European countries in private investment.

Many Japanese executives have said they are not comfortable with Indian business culture and complex legal system. But they have predicted that once leading Japanese firms decide to put down stakes in India, there will be a rush.
Toyota's chief Toyoda said he hoped he hoped to meet officials of Indian financial group Kirloskar, a possible joint venture partner, while in India.
Last month Toyota director Hideaki Otaka said the Japanese company was in talks with Kirloskar to form a joint venture car plant in a location still to be decided.
The Keidanren leaders said they continued to press India to scrap red tape which they said discourages investors.

"The level of development of the legal system has been very high, maybe too much and that has led to excessive regulations," Toyoda said. "There is a need for elimination and relaxation of regulations so that we can enhance free competition."
Miyoshi said Indian bureaucrats required cumbersome procedures, and the system for granting licences was complicated. "The process is quite time-consuming," he said.
